notebooks.title: Foundational Constraints in AI Metareasoning
notebooks.summary: AI metareasoning is currently bifurcated: established 'resource partition' models focus on computational efficiency, while emerging epistemological frameworks like 'Equity Bias' advocate for making foundational assumptions explicit and contestable. Current LLMs can support the transparency of these assumptions, but autonomous self-correction of foundational premises remains unproven.
notebooks.findings:
Traditional metareasoning focuses on the 'partition problem' of resource allocation rather than epistemic self-correction. [source-27c3e6da377b41e4]

Epistemic inclusion frameworks offer a strategy for making AI foundational assumptions 'contestable' rather than invisible. [source-443f82fd8d5543a6]
notebooks.limitations: Evidence remains concentrated in theoretical frameworks or external design methodologies; there is no documented empirical proof of an LLM autonomously identifying a foundational logical flaw in its own reasoning architecture and developing a superior replacement without human intervention.
notebooks.next_questions: Can the 'Equity Bias' framework's 'Equity Archaeology' methodology be implemented as an automated internal loop within an LLM's chain-of-thought to detect invalid premise propagation?
notebooks.reason: Revising the notebook to incorporate the 'Equity Bias' framework provides a clearer pathway to addressing the project's question on assumption identification.

review.alternative: Metareasoning could encompass self-correction, but the literature has prioritized efficiency (partitioning) for decades.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of significant research focus on autonomous internal consistency checking in the 1990s-2010s.

claims.statement: Traditional metareasoning focuses on the 'partition problem' of resource allocation rather than epistemic self-correction.

support.explanation: This establishes that foundational research in metareasoning is primarily about performance trade-offs, not belief truth-tracking.
support.passage: We shall introduce the metareasoning-partition problem--the problem of ideally apportioning costly reasoning resources to planning a solution versus applying resource to executing a solution to a problem.

review.alternative: Transparency does not equal autonomous self-correction; the model might expose assumptions but not reform them.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that the Equity Bias framework is purely a human-in-the-loop audit protocol with no path to automation.

claims.statement: Epistemic inclusion frameworks offer a strategy for making AI foundational assumptions 'contestable' rather than invisible.

support.explanation: This framework suggests that identifying foundational assumptions is a design requirement for accountability, potentially providing a model for how an AI could expose its own premises.
support.passage: While traditional approaches aim to reduce or remove bias, Equity Bias instead makes bias transparent and contestable. In doing so, it broadens whose perspectives shape AI and provides a lens for understanding AI systems as interpretive agents.

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

detail.title: Foundational Constraints in AI Metareasoning
detail.summary: AI metareasoning is currently bifurcated: established 'resource partition' models focus on computational efficiency, while emerging epistemological frameworks like 'Equity Bias' advocate for making foundational assumptions explicit and contestable. Current LLMs can support the transparency of these assumptions, but autonomous self-correction of foundational premises remains unproven.
detail.findings:
Traditional metareasoning focuses on the 'partition problem' of resource allocation rather than epistemic self-correction. [source-27c3e6da377b41e4]

Epistemic inclusion frameworks offer a strategy for making AI foundational assumptions 'contestable' rather than invisible. [source-443f82fd8d5543a6]
detail.limitations: Evidence remains concentrated in theoretical frameworks or external design methodologies; there is no documented empirical proof of an LLM autonomously identifying a foundational logical flaw in its own reasoning architecture and developing a superior replacement without human intervention.
detail.next_questions: Can the 'Equity Bias' framework's 'Equity Archaeology' methodology be implemented as an automated internal loop within an LLM's chain-of-thought to detect invalid premise propagation?
detail.reason: Revising the notebook to incorporate the 'Equity Bias' framework provides a clearer pathway to addressing the project's question on assumption identification.

support.passage: We shall introduce the metareasoning-partition problem--the problem of ideally apportioning costly reasoning resources to planning a solution versus applying resource to executing a solution to a problem.

review.alternative: Transparency does not equal autonomous self-correction; the model might expose assumptions but not reform them.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that the Equity Bias framework is purely a human-in-the-loop audit protocol with no path to automation.

claims.statement: Epistemic inclusion frameworks offer a strategy for making AI foundational assumptions 'contestable' rather than invisible.

support.explanation: This framework suggests that identifying foundational assumptions is a design requirement for accountability, potentially providing a model for how an AI could expose its own premises.
support.passage: While traditional approaches aim to reduce or remove bias, Equity Bias instead makes bias transparent and contestable. In doing so, it broadens whose perspectives shape AI and provides a lens for understanding AI systems as interpretive agents.
